slides.title: Judging the film
bullets: The film should not be thick.
There should be no ragged edges and no lengthwise or crosswise streaks.
There should be no empty patches (a sign that the slide was not properly degreased).
A correctly made dry film is thin, yellowish and ends 1–1.5 cm from the edge.
If the volume of blood is always the same and it is spread evenly on the same part of the slide, staining and reading are standardised — hence the pear-shaped pipette.

slides.title: Sources of error
bullets: If the fixing alcohol contains water, the cells are not fixed in the proper shape.
For the differential count the pH of the buffered water must be 6.8–7.2.
In a thick, uneven film the cells are hard to describe: the red cells are altered and the leukocytes gather at the edges.
A badly made, badly fixed or badly stained film is the main cause of errors in recognising cells.

slides.title: Criteria for identifying a cell
bullets: Compare the size of the leukocyte with red cells and note its shape.
Assess the shape, structure and size of the nucleus relative to the whole cell, the density of the nucleus and its position (central or at the edge).
Note the appearance and colour of the cytoplasm and of all granules.
Determine the nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio.
Check whether any vacuoles are present (stained or unstained).
Learn to recognise normal cells correctly — then you will be able to detect abnormal leukocytes.

slides.title: Sources of error
bullets: Visual differential counting has three main sources of error: uneven distribution of cells in the preparation, failure to recognise cells, and statistics (the number of cells counted).
In an ordinary film neutrophils, monocytes and eosinophils lie more at the edges and lymphocytes in the middle, so the film is moved in one direction.
A badly made, badly fixed or badly stained film is the main cause of errors in recognising cells.
Counting an abnormal cell among the “normal” ones is a serious error; films with abnormalities go to the senior specialist of the laboratory for the final decision.

slides.title: Calculation and result
bullets: Platelets (× 10⁹/L) = red cells (× 10¹²/L) × the number of platelets per 1000 red cells.
Normal by the Fonio method: 45–70 ‰ against 1000 red cells.
Thrombocytopenia is a fall, and thrombocytosis a rise, of the platelet count outside the reference interval.
Thrombocytosis may be reactive (secondary — e.g. in inflammation or blood loss) or primary (a bone-marrow disease); the platelet count alone does not tell them apart.
There are many causes (blood diseases, blood loss, inflammation, drugs and others) — interpret together with the clinical data.

slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: The red-cell count per µL of blood must be known beforehand for the calculation — a wrong red-cell count also distorts the platelet count.
The result depends on the quality of the smear and correct staining: it must be even, fixed and stained by Romanowsky–Giemsa (see the smear preparation and staining protocol).
Compare with other methods (Goryaev chamber, automatic analyser) and repeat if the discrepancy is large.
Capillary blood may be used to determine the platelet count (see the blood collection protocol for haemostasis).

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.caption: White blood cell at the centre (neutrophil): white cells are typically seen in a peripheral blood smear. Neutrophils are a type of white cell and one of the body's main defences against infection; finding them in a smear is normal. Numerous red blood cells: they carry oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and return carbon dioxide to the lungs.
slides.credit: Photo: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya, CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.caption: Many red cells in a smear are normal; a high number may be linked to polycythaemia or dehydration. Platelets (dot-like bodies): small cell fragments involved in clotting and wound healing, seen as small dots. A normal platelet number is essential for clotting; low counts (thrombocytopenia) or abnormal function can cause bleeding disorders.
slides.credit: Photo: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya, CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.caption: At 1000X magnification, this blood smear photomicrograph shows an eosinophilic leukocyte (arrowhead), or eosinophil, a type of white cell. Polymorphonuclear because of its multilobed nucleus, it is classed as a granulocyte because of the granules in its cytoplasm. It is surrounded by numerous red blood cells.
slides.credit: Photo: CDC/ Dr. F. Gilbert, CDC PHIL · CDC Public Health Image Library

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.caption: At 1000X magnification, this blood smear photomicrograph shows a basophilic leukocyte (arrowhead), or basophil, a type of white cell. Polymorphonuclear (PMN) because of its multilobed nucleus, which is hard to see here, it is classed as a granulocyte because of the abundant large granules in its cytoplasm. It is surrounded by numerous red blood cells.
slides.credit: Photo: CDC/ Dr. F. Gilbert, CDC PHIL · CDC Public Health Image Library
